title: AI Agents for Teachers
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky traces how "AI agents" evolved from thin, failure-prone 2024 demos to genuinely capable but underused tools, arguing education is stuck relitigating AI literacy while agentic systems already run critical functions in business. He unpacks agent failure modes via Alejandro Piad Morffis's framework, then narrates a concrete Claude Cowork workflow - a Drive-connected source-and-standards sweep for unit planning - to show teachers what agentic use actually looks like beyond a single chat prompt. His central move is distinguishing degrees of agency (data access, permission to write, scheduled autonomy, and depth of delegated deliberation) rather than treating "more agentic" as one linear scale. He closes by arguing that human evaluation doesn't shrink as agents get more capable - it relocates to fewer, higher-stakes checkpoints - and previews a follow-up piece on student-facing agentic workflows.
points: Agentic loops fail differently than single chats: they amplify hallucinations into cascading faulty frameworks, waste tokens when a single chat would have sufficed, and drift unchecked without an external verifier.

Agency is not one ladder - Potkalitsky separates what a system can see (data access), what it can change (write permission), when it can act (scheduled autonomy), and how much deliberation it is delegated, arguing these vary independently rather than scaling together.

His concrete example - a Drive-connected 'source-and-standards sweep' inside a Cowork project - models a low-risk entry point for teachers: read-only search across an instructional archive before granting write access.
The riskiest layer is delegated deliberation, not file access or scheduling: once an agent's judgment feeds forward into later steps, small errors compound silently.
Human evaluation doesn't shrink as agentic capability grows - it moves to fewer, higher-stakes checkpoints where the teacher decides what counts as a good result.
quotes: I have been writing about AI agents and education since 2024, back when toolmakers were calling it “the year of the agent.

First, agentic loops amplify hallucinations. A user can catch and reroute a misleading sentence in a single chat cycle. In an agentic loop, hallucinations cascade into faulty belief structures and analytical frameworks that can lead to serious missteps in action and evaluation.
Claude for Teachers represents the first breakthrough in teacher use of agentic AI. The platform comes with ample reassurances about data privacy and safety.

One distinction is simply what the system is allowed to do. In the workflow above, Claude can read from the archive but cannot change it. Give it permission to create a file in the designated Drive folder, and something important changes.
The distinctive risk of an agentic workflow is not simply that Claude can touch more files or run while you are away from the computer. It is that a loop can carry its own judgments forward.
This is also why human evaluation does not become less important as the workflow becomes more capable. It changes location.
A questionable source selection becomes part of a unit draft. A weak interpretation of an instructional priority shapes the next recommendation.
